rv.q: Giles Croft’s production captures the heart of the story, and in turn the hearts of its audience, with a quietly impressive, and ultimately overwhelming, theatrical authority.
And in this year of all years, it’s great to see a compassionate story about asylum seekers from the Middle East on our stage, and with a great BAME cast to boot.
It’s a performance of brooding intensity, alive to the moral and emotional intricacies of Amir’s journey.
The touching story of the novel is carried on stage by the turbulent ups and downs, echoing the ducking and diving of a fighting kite that will come up winning.
The evening still casts a spell, particularly in the first half, when we’re introduced to the psychological, ethnic and religious threads that will become more tangled as darker forces loom larger.
“But is it a West End production?” the woman behind me quizzed her neighbours — obviously all theatre people — as they took their seats for the second half.
If melodramatic sagas are your bag, you may well enjoy this show, despite a few moments of frightful corn in Matthew Spangler’s script.
If I’m honest, however, I got far more satisfaction from reading the book than from watching this devout distillation of it.
Bright spots that can’t make up for the ploddiness elsewhere.
The Kite Runner is worth seeing.
This at least partially disguises the fall in energy and urgency of the play's second act, which simply has too much ground to cover before it reaches the dramatic events of its close.

The Kite Runner, a novel by Khaled Hosseini, has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide. Now it arrives on the West End stage, a doggedly efficient piece that somehow lacks true dazzle. The narrative style involves thick wodges of plot being delivered at the audience like news bulletins on the half-hour.
Giles Croft’s beautifully measured production does full justice to the play’s many moods, creating particularly lyrical images of the kites.
But it is the story rather than the production that moves you to tears.
But somehow it remains a competent affair well enough directed by Giles Croft which fails to move the heart, something both novel and film achieved.

cn.t: A workmanlike adaptation of Hosseini's bestseller delivers efficient, emotional storytelling but lacks theatrical dazzle. Critics find it faithful to the novel yet struggles to soar onstage, though many audiences are moved to tears.
